title: Rabboni (John 20:11–18)
hook: Mary turns at her name, and becomes the apostle to the apostles

segments.voice: Yesterday, two friends racing at dawn. Your line was they both ran. Whose good news did you run toward? Day six hundred fifty-one.

The two men have gone home. Mary Magdalene hasn't. She's standing outside the tomb, crying. She stoops and looks in, and there are two angels in white, sitting where the body had been, one at the head and one at the feet. They ask her: woman, why are you weeping? And she answers as if angels were the most ordinary thing in the world, because grief is louder than wonder. They have taken away my Lord, and I don't know where they've laid him. Then she turns around, and someone is standing there.
screen: `TWO ANGELS, AND GRIEF LOUDER THAN WONDER.`

segments.voice: She doesn't recognize him. John says she supposed him to be the gardener. And she asks: sir, if you've carried him off, tell me where, and I'll take him away. Then one word. In the King James Bible: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master." Her name. That's all it takes. Back in chapter ten, he said the good shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they know his voice. Here it happens. Rabboni is Aramaic, a warm form of rabbi, my teacher, my master. Then he says something people have puzzled over: "Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father." In Latin, noli me tangere, and painters loved it. The Greek may mean something closer to stop clinging to me, don't hold on: there's somewhere to go and a message to carry. And he gives her the message. Go to my brothers. So she goes, and in the Greek she says it in her own voice: I have seen the Lord. She's the first person in John's Gospel to see the risen Jesus, and the first sent to tell. Early Christian writers called her the apostle to the apostles, the one sent to those who would be sent. In 2016, Pope Francis raised her day, July twenty-second, to a full feast. Orthodox Christians call her equal to the apostles. One more thing worth clearing up: the idea that Mary Magdalene was a reformed prostitute isn't in the Gospels. It grew from a sixth-century sermon that merged her with other women. The Gospels themselves remember her as a witness. This week: thorns and purple, a seamless robe, it is finished, blood and water, myrrh, a race, and now a name.
screen: then, large: `I HAVE SEEN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say I have seen the Lord, or as much of it as is true for you. Settle, and breathe. Remember being called by name by someone who loved you. A parent at the door. A friend across a crowded room. Feel what your own name sounds like in their voice. Then, if you're a Christian, you can say Mary's words quietly: I have seen the Lord. If you're not, think of something good you've seen with your own eyes this week, and say it out loud: I have seen that. The bell holds the time.
Rabboni. Aramaic for my teacher: what Mary says when she hears her name and turns.
Your line: I have seen the lord. Today, use someone's name warmly, on purpose, and tell one person about something good you've seen. Day six hundred fifty-one, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene on July 22, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles; many churches read this passage during the Easter season.

fork.setup: you're Mary, weeping at the tomb. a man you take for the gardener asks why you're crying. what do you say?
options: sir, if you've carried him off, tell me where, and I'll take him.
fork.reveal: she asks the gardener for the body, and then he says one word: Mary. she turns: Rabboni.

original.note: Greek spelling of an Aramaic word: my teacher, my master. a warmer form of rabbi.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mary calls him teacher.
what it means: grief so loud she mistakes him for the gardener, until he says her name, and she's the first one sent to tell.
what a scholar hears: rabbouni, Aramaic, and the Latin 'apostola apostolorum', apostle to the apostles. the 'penitent prostitute' idea comes from Gregory the Great's homily of 591, not the Gospels.

notes: KJV 20:18 is indirect speech ('that she had seen the Lord'); the Greek is first person (heoraka ton kyrion). Script says 'in the Greek she says it in her own voice'. Confirm.
'Apostle to the apostles': associated with Hippolytus (3rd c.) and used by Thomas Aquinas and others. Script says 'early Christian writers'. Confirm.
2016 elevation of the July 22 memorial to a feast by Pope Francis. Confirm.
Gregory the Great's Homily 33 (591) merging Mary Magdalene with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and Mary of Bethany. Confirm.
Noli me tangere: 'stop clinging' reading of the present imperative is common; stated as 'may mean'.
Practice adapts the outline ('say I have seen the lord') as an invitation. Confirm it is appropriately optional.
